question: For each of the 50 states, plus D.C. and Puerto Rico, answered as one set: when campaign-finance misconduct from before taking office is found against a sitting governor, which routes can act on it and how? (1) Impeachment: the standard (is pre-office conduct impeachable?), which body impeaches and which tries, and the vote thresholds. (2) Recall: whether the state allows recall of a governor, the grounds, the signature threshold and timing. (3) Criminal referral: who prosecutes a sitting governor for state campaign-finance crimes, and whether any immunity or delay applies. (4) Removal or disqualification: any court-ordered removal, forfeiture of office or bar from future office. Then, from real cases, which routes were actually used against governors or other statewide officials for campaign-fund misuse, and what scale of misuse triggered each. Mark anything not found as UNKNOWN.
requestedBy: A corrupt life in power playtest thread, filed by the research intake thread

sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: It covers how misconduct is detected federally, not what happens to someone already in office.

title: What can happen to a sitting governor found to have misused campaign funds before taking office
usableAnswer: A 52-row table of impeachment standard, bodies and thresholds; recall availability, grounds and threshold; prosecutor and any immunity; removal or disqualification; with citations and evidence status; plus a short list of real cases with the route used and the amount involved.
whyItMatters: In play, Lucia Moran became Governor of Alaska after taking about $154,000 from her campaign in 43 withdrawals over ten months. The game now fines her and orders repayment during the campaign, but nothing follows her into office: no impeachment, recall, prosecution or removal route exists for a sitting governor. lamontae asked how the scandal played out and whether she could avoid getting caught.
